bes0: Fifth Metatarsal Fracture (Outer Edge of the Foot): Healing, Boot and Exercises | İhsan Eren
bes1: A break on the outer edge of the foot: how long a fifth metatarsal fracture takes to heal, when to stop wearing the boot and why a Jones fracture is different. Recovery week by week and six exercises.
bes2: Fifth metatarsal fracture (outer edge of the foot)
bes3: Do you have pain and swelling on the outer edge of your foot, along the long bone leading to the little toe, after going over on your foot? This bone is the fifth metatarsal. Most of these fractures heal without problems: the bone knits in about 6 weeks, and walking as far as pain allows helps recovery. This page explains what to watch out for with each type of fracture and the exercises you can do at home.

bes11: Breaks at the end of the bone nearest the ankle. A boot or rigid-soled shoe is for comfort only; you can walk on the foot as far as pain allows. Use crutches if you need them.
bes13: Near the base, but slightly further along. It may heal more slowly: in the first weeks you may be in a cast with crutches and not put weight on the foot. A small number do not heal and may need surgery.
bes15: Breaks in the middle part of the bone. The boot is usually for comfort, and walking as far as is comfortable is encouraged; walking on your heel may be easier at first.

bes19: Weeks 0–3: Wear the boot when walking and take it off when resting and at night. Put weight on the foot as pain allows, and stop using crutches when you feel ready.
bes20: Weeks 3–6: Gradually wear the boot less and return to your usual tasks.
bes21: Weeks 6–12: Most people return to their usual activities; long walks and running may still cause discomfort and swelling for a while.

bes27: Six exercises to keep your foot and ankle moving
bes28: Start the first four exercises as early as you can, without making your pain noticeably worse. The last two are done standing: start them once you can walk comfortably. With a Jones fracture, wait for your team’s approval before doing standing exercises.
bes29: Pull your foot up and push it down as far as is comfortable. Moving early supports circulation and reduces the risk of a blood clot in the leg.

bes46: Does the boot help the fracture heal?
bes47: For fractures at the base of the bone, the boot or rigid-soled shoe is given only for comfort; it does not speed up healing. Wear it when walking, and you can take it off when resting and at night. Wearing a supportive shoe on your uninjured foot protects your other joints.
bes48: What is a Jones fracture, and why is it treated differently?
bes49: A Jones fracture is a break near the base of the fifth metatarsal but slightly further along, and it may heal more slowly. According to one NHS leaflet, for the first 6 weeks you wear a cast and use crutches without putting weight on the foot; after that you may move into a boot. A small number of these fractures do not heal on their own, and surgery may be considered. Your team will tell you your fracture type and how much weight you can put on it.
bes50: When you are out of the boot or rigid-soled shoe, can walk comfortably, can do emergency manoeuvres such as an emergency stop without pain or hesitation, and your insurance covers you. Try it in a safe place first.
bes51: When you can squat, hop, jump and run without pain. Most people return to their usual activities within 6–12 weeks; more demanding activities such as running may cause discomfort for a while longer. If you can’t do these things, see your doctor about physiotherapy.
bes52: How long do pain and swelling last?
bes53: The fracture heals in about 6 weeks, but pain and swelling can last 3–6 months. Swelling is usually worse at the end of the day and should improve clearly from week 4. Smoking slows healing and in extreme cases can stop it.
